reading.rtitle: The Email He Reads at Six
paras: An American executive opens his inbox before six in the morning, on a phone, standing up, and he decides about each message in about eight seconds. In those eight seconds he reads two things: the subject line and the first sentence. Everything else you wrote is read only if those two survive. This is the opposite of the way most of us were taught to write. At school we built the argument first and put the conclusion at the end, so that the reader arrived there with us. In American professional writing the conclusion goes at the top, and everything after it exists to support it. The name for that habit is bottom line up front. It feels blunt the first time you do it, and it is not: it is a service to a recipient with ninety other messages behind yours. If there is nothing to decide, three lines to acknowledge the message are enough, and the sign-off does the rest.

The second difference is the register itself, and this is where written English stops behaving like spoken English. When we speak, we use verbs: we decided to move the date, the vendor failed twice, I reviewed the contract on Monday. When we write at a senior level, those events become nouns: the decision to move the date, two vendor failures, my review of the contract. The move has a name, nominalization, and it is why a written sentence can carry a whole event in its subject and still sound calm. It is also the most dangerous tool in the box, because a noun does not need an actor. The delay was not communicated tells the reader almost nothing: nobody delayed anything, nobody stayed silent, and there is nothing to answer. We did not tell the client for two days tells him everything, including who is writing to him. Use the noun to package what you both already agree on. Bring the verb back, with a person in front of it, the moment somebody has to act or answer for something.

After that the shape is almost mechanical, and the follow-up email after an interview is the clearest example of it. The subject line names the thing. The first line picks up something the other person said, not something about you, so that the message is a continuation and not a broadcast. The bottom line comes next, in one sentence. Two or three lines carry the evidence, and each of them has to be concise, which is not the same as short: short is about the number of words, concise is about waste. A wordy paragraph is not more polite; it only moves the work to the reader. Then comes one clear ask, and only one, because two questions in a single message get one answer and it is always the easier one. Finally the sign-off, chosen as carefully as the subject line, because it sets the distance for the next message as well. Send it inside twenty-four hours, and never open with I hope this email finds you well: the reader has already deleted four of those this morning.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: A professional email in English should be as long and as polite as possible, so that the reader feels respected before the point arrives.
In American professional writing the bottom line goes first, and the writer chooses between the noun, which packages what is agreed, and the verb, which keeps the actor visible.
The safest way to write to a senior reader is to build the argument slowly and leave the conclusion for the last paragraph, exactly as we were taught at school.

gapfill.text: Two rules carry the whole lesson. Put the bottom line first, so that the reader can stop after one sentence and still know what you want. Then choose: the decision was made packages what you both already agree on, and we decided keeps you visible. Wherever somebody has to act, the verb comes back and brings the person with it.

bank.label: Lines that do the work
items: Follow-up: AI safety role, Thursday interview
You said the first year would be judged on the review cycle.
The bottom line: I would take the role, and I could start in six weeks.
Two numbers from Thursday, in case they help.
The platform replacement ran for nineteen months.
We told the client late, and that one is on me.
Could you let me know whether the peer conversation changes the timeline?
Happy to send a one-page version if that is easier to read on a phone.
Best regards,

forms.title: Five moves that make written English sound senior
cards: Say the conclusion before the evidence. The reader can stop after the first line and still know what you want, and nobody has ever complained about being told too early.
we decided becomes the decision, the vendor failed twice becomes two vendor failures. Use it for what you both already agree on, and the sentence stays calm and short.
The verb that keeps the actor
The delay was not communicated hides everyone. We did not tell the client for two days names the writer. Where there is an action or a responsibility, the verb comes back.
The last line before the sign-off
Two questions in one email produce one answer, and it is always the easier one. Ask for the thing you actually need and leave the rest for the next message.
Best regards is safe with someone you have met once. Best is warmer and normal in an American office. Thanks only works when you really are asking for something.

items.situation: You interviewed on Thursday and it is Friday morning. Say the subject line of your follow-up email out loud.
tips: Follow-up: AI safety role, Thursday interview
It names the thing and the day. No thank-you, no adjectives, nothing the reader has to open the message to understand.

items.situation: Your first line has to pick up something he said, not something about you. Say it.
tips: You said the first year would be judged on how fast the review cycle moves.
That makes the email a continuation of Thursday instead of a broadcast that could have gone to anyone.

items.situation: Say this in one sentence, bottom line first: you want the role, you could start in six weeks, and one more conversation with the peer team would help.
tips: The bottom line: I would take the role, and I could start in six weeks -- one more conversation with the peer team would help me arrive ready.
The decision comes first. The condition comes after it, never in front of it.

items.situation: Turn this spoken sentence into one written sentence built on a noun: We decided to move the deadline because the vendor failed twice.
tips: The decision to move the deadline followed two vendor failures.
Two verbs became two nouns, and the sentence lost eight words without losing anything else.

items.situation: Now repair this written sentence, which hides everyone: The delay was not communicated to the client.
tips: We did not tell the client about the delay for two days.
There is responsibility in this sentence, so the verb has to come back and bring the person with it.

items: Round 1 -- Guided
Dictate the subject line and the first two sentences of your follow-up email. Your teacher writes down exactly what you say and nothing else, so you see your own draft.
Round 2 -- The middle
Add the bottom line and two lines of evidence. Every line has to survive one question: if I delete this, what would the reader miss?
Round 3 -- One ask, one sign-off
Close with a single question and a sign-off, then read the whole message out loud from the top, as the reader would at six in the morning.
Curveball
Your teacher tells you the reader is the recruiter, not the hiring manager. Say which two lines change, and why compensation only belongs in one of the two emails.

answerkey.title: Reveal the marked-up model email
list: Subject: Follow-up -- AI safety role, Thursday interview [THE LABEL: it says what is inside, and the day locates it in his week]
"You said the first year would be judged on how fast the review cycle moves." [THE OPENING: his sentence, not mine -- this is a continuation, not a broadcast]
"The bottom line: I would take the role, and I could start in six weeks." [BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: he can stop here and still know everything he needs]
"The platform replacement ran for nineteen months and cut the release cycle from six weeks to nine days." [THE NOUN: the replacement packages an event we both already agree on]
"The failed program cost us two quarters, and we told the client late -- that one is on me." [THE VERB COMES BACK: there is responsibility here, so there is a person in front of the verb]
"Could you let me know whether the peer conversation changes the timeline on your side?" [ONE ASK, and it is his to answer -- compensation goes to the recruiter, never here]
"Best regards, Lucia Nishiyama Serra" [THE SIGN-OFF: met once, decided the process, so warm is wrong and cold is worse]
answerkey.note: Read the model once, then compare it with your own version. What matters is the ORDER of the lines and the choice between noun and verb -- not these exact words.

listenings.text: I have been rewriting emails for senior people for about twelve years, and the first thing I do with almost every one of them is the same. I delete the opening paragraph. Not because it is badly written, but because it is almost never the beginning. The real first sentence is usually the second one, and everything before it is the writer clearing his throat in public. I hope this finds you well. I wanted to reach out. Following up on our conversation of last week. None of that is information, and the reader has seen all three before breakfast. Now, the word people always give me back is short. They tell me they will make it shorter, and that is not what I asked for. Short is about how many words there are. Concise is about how many of them are doing work. I have read four-line emails that were wordy, because three of the lines said nothing, and I have read a full page that was concise, because every paragraph carried something the reader needed to decide. So here is the test I use, and it is the only editing rule I would give anybody who writes in a second language. Take one line out. Then ask what the reader would miss. If the honest answer is nothing, the line does not go back in. Do that four or five times and you will find the strange thing: the email gets shorter and it also gets warmer, because what is left is all about the person reading it.

Quick note for the team, and I am recording it because I keep saying it one person at a time. Here is what actually happens with your emails. I read them on my phone, standing in the kitchen, before six, before anybody in this building is awake. That is my inbox hour. I make a decision about each message in a few seconds, and there are only three of them: answer now, keep it for later, or archive it. And I want you to know exactly what sends a message to archive. It is not bad grammar. I do not care about your grammar, half of this company writes in a second language and some of the clearest writing I get comes from people who learned English at thirty. What sends it to archive is this: two lines have gone by and I still do not know what you want from me. If I have to read to the bottom of a message to find the question, I will not do it at ten to six, and I will not come back to it at eleven either, because by then there are sixty more. Second thing, and this one is a favor to yourselves. Ask me one thing. When there are two questions in a message I answer the easy one, every time, and I promise you I am not doing it on purpose. And the last one. When something has gone wrong, write it with a person in it. There was a communication gap tells me nothing and it makes me suspicious. We missed it and here is what we changed tells me who I am talking to, and that email gets an answer before I put the phone down.

extra_audio.text: First I write the subject line, because it forces me to know what the message is really about. Then I open with something the other person said, so it reads as a continuation. After that I put the bottom line in one sentence, before any evidence. Then I add two short lines of proof, and I delete anything the reader would not miss. And I close with one question and a sign-off, and I send it the same day.
